title: Crash-Safe Saves
content:
Crash-Safe Saves Writing straight to the final path is risky: if the process crashes mid-write, the file is left half-written and the old data is gone. The fix is to write to a temporary file first and then rename it over the target. On most filesystems a rename within the same directory is atomic — readers see either the complete old file or the complete new file, never a mix. The temp file must live in the same directory as the target, because only same-directory renames are guaranteed atomic (a cross-directory rename may silently become a slow, non-atomic copy).

title: Mutex Counter
content:
Mutex Counter One hundred goroutines adding to one integer is the classic shared-state race: c.n += n looks like a single step but compiles to load, add, store, so two goroutines can overwrite each other and increments get lost. The fix is a sync.Mutex on the struct — Add and Value each lock, touch n, and unlock (usually with defer), so only one goroutine holds the count at a time. That is the Go equivalent of the shared-counter step in the Rust course this section is adapted from.

title: Struct
content:
Struct A Go struct groups related fields into one value. Think of it as the skeleton for every domain type in this course — Ticket today, TicketStore and HTTP handlers later.
Why this matters Go has no classes and no inheritance. Composition starts with structs: bundle data, attach methods with receivers, construct via functions like NewTicket. Master the literal syntax once and the rest of the course reads easily.
type Ticket struct { Title string Description string } tk := Ticket{Title: "Fix bug", Description: "Crash on login"} fmt.Println(tk.Title) // "Fix bug"Construction styles Always prefer named fields (order-independent, future-proof):
// Good: survives field reordering and additions a := Ticket{Title: "A", Description: "B"} // Fragile: positional — breaks if fields move b := Ticket{"A", "B"} // Zero value: missing fields default to "" / 0 / nil / false c := Ticket{Title: "A"} // c.Description == ""The NewTicket pattern is idiomatic Go — there are no constructors:
func NewTicket(title, description string) Ticket { return Ticket{Title: title, Description: description} }Later you will see it return (Ticket, error) when validation is added.
Exporting: capital letter = public There are no pub / private keywords in Go. The first letter decides:
type Ticket struct { Title string // exported: visible as ticket.Ticket.Title notes string // unexported: only usable inside package ticket }Same rule for functions, types, and methods: NewTicket is usable from another package, newTicket is not.
Common pitfalls Positional literals: Ticket{"A", "B"} compiles but rots. go vet flags some cases — use named fields. Copy semantics: structs are values. u := tk copies both strings (cheap headers). Mutating u.Title does not touch tk. Pass *Ticket when you need shared mutation. Unexported fields from outside: ticket.Ticket{notes: "..."} outside package ticket fails to compile. That is intentional encapsulation — expose a constructor instead. == surprises: structs with only comparable fields support ==, but slices/maps inside make it illegal. You will hit this in the store exercises. Go vs Rust Rust: pub struct Ticket { pub title: String } — pub per item. Go: type Ticket struct { Title string } — capital per name. Rust’s Ticket { title, description } shorthand matches Go’s Ticket{Title: title, Description: description} almost line for line.
Trivia Go structs can be compared, copied, and embedded — embedding (type Queue struct { Ticket }) gives method promotion, Go’s answer to inheritance. fmt.Printf("%+v", tk) prints field names plus values, which is why tests use t.Fatalf("got %+v", tk) for readable failures.
Tip: when a test prints got { }, you returned the zero value. Check that NewTicket actually assigns both parameters to fields.

title: Syntax
content:
Syntax Every Go file starts with a package clause, then declares functions with func. This exercise is your first look at that skeleton — the same shape you will see in all 100 exercises.
Why this matters Go is deliberately small. If you can read a function signature you can read most Go programs: typed inputs on the left, return type on the right, body in braces. No classes, no exceptions, no hidden control flow.
package syntax func Compute(a, b int) int { return a + b } package syntax declares which package this file belongs to. Every .go file in one folder must agree on the name. func starts a function declaration. (a, b int) is shorthand for (a int, b int) — two int parameters. The trailing int is the return type. return a + b exits with a value. More examples Parameters with different types each need their own type:
func Greet(name string, times int) string { if times <= 1 { return "Hello, " + name } return "Hello, " + name + "!" }Multiple return values are normal in Go (errors use this):
func DivMod(a, b int) (quot, rem int) { quot = a / b rem = a % b return quot, rem // or just `return` — named results are pre-declared }No return value means no trailing type:
func Log(msg string) { println(msg) }Common pitfalls Missing return: if you declare -> int (i.e. int result), every code path must return a value. The compiler rejects it otherwise. Unused variables: x := 5 then never using x is a compile error. Delete it or use _ = x while experimenting. := vs =: := declares a new variable, = assigns. Inside func you usually see sum := a + b. Go vs Rust Rust uses fn greeting() -> &'static str { ... } with the last expression returned implicitly. Go spells it func Greeting() string { return ... } — return is always explicit, and there is no implicit tail-expression return.
Trivia Go’s func keyword comes from C’s func heritage via Plan 9 and Limbo. gofmt (run gofmt -l .) enforces one canonical layout, so Go code looks the same everywhere — tabs, not spaces.
Tip: run go vet ./exercises/01_intro/01_syntax/ after editing. It catches signature mistakes faster than reading test output.

title: Channel Pipeline
content:
Channel Pipeline A channel lets goroutines hand values back to the code that launched them: each worker computes one result and sends it, and the caller collects the sends into the output slice. The trick is keeping input order — send each result tagged with its index (or write directly to out[i] from the worker) and wait for every goroutine before returning. That is the Go equivalent of the message-passing step in the Rust course this section is adapted from.

title: Loading State at Boot
content:
Loading State at Boot Servers usually reload their state from disk when they start, but on the very first run there is no file yet — and that is normal, not a crash. The convention is to treat a missing file as empty state: return (nil, nil) and let the caller start fresh. Any other error (permissions, a directory in the way) is still a real error. Go reports a missing file through os.IsNotExist, which recognizes the “not exist” error even when it is wrapped.

title: Map Store
content:
Map Store A map gives indexed lookup: one key leads straight to its value instead of scanning every element. title: Writing Lines
content:
Writing Lines An io.Writer is the mirror of a reader: you hand it bytes and it reports how many it accepted, returning an error if something went wrong. title: Buffered Collect
content:

A buffered channel make(chan int, n) lets up to n sends complete without a waiting receiver — ideal for fan-out/collect: launch n goroutines, each computes one value and sends it, then the caller drains the channel into the output slice in order. title: Slice Functions (Clone)
content:

A true clone needs a fresh array with the elements copied over; the standard library offers slices.Clone by name for exactly this, and the manual equivalent is an append-into-empty or copy-into-made slice. This is the Go equivalent of the cloning step in the ticket-store section of the Rust course this section is adapted from.

title: Overflow
content:
Overflow A uint8 holds 0 to 255. Add past the top and Go does not panic — it wraps around modulo 256. That silent wrap is the whole bug class this exercise trains you to spot.
Why this matters Counters, checksums, pixel values, and protocol lengths often use small unsigned types. In production a wrap becomes a wrong length, an index out of range, or a security check that passes when it should fail. Go leaves the check to you.
var a uint8 = 200 var b uint8 = 100 sum := a + b // 44, not 300: (200+100) % 256 == 44Detecting the wrap For addition, the wrap test is one comparison:
func AddUint8(a, b uint8) (sum uint8, overflow bool) { sum = a + b overflow = sum < a // wrapped iff result is smaller than an input return sum, overflow }Why does sum < a work? Without wrap, sum = a + b >= a. With wrap, 256 is subtracted, so sum = a + b - 256 < a (since b < 256).
More examples:
AddUint8(100, 100) // (200, false) — fits AddUint8(200, 100) // (44, true) — wrapped AddUint8(255, 1) // (0, true) — classic edgeFor wider code, prefer the standard library instead of hand-rolling (Add works on uint; sized variants stop at 32/64 — there is no Add8):
import "math/bits" sum, carry := bits.Add(uint(200), uint(100), 0) // sum=300, carry=0 → no overflow for uint width. // For uint8 specifically, check the 8-bit range or use the wide-type // version below; carry==1 would mean overflow for that width.Or sidestep it by computing in a bigger type:
func AddUint8Wide(a, b uint8) (uint8, bool) { w := uint16(a) + uint16(b) if w > 255 { return uint8(w), true } return uint8(w), false }Common pitfalls Signed vs unsigned: int8(120) + 20 also wraps (to -116), but sum < a only works for unsigned. Signed overflow needs math/bits or range checks before adding. Assuming a panic: Go never panics on integer overflow — debug or release. If you come from Rust, drop the expectation. Wider-type amnesia: uint8(a+b) where a, b int already overflowed int logic is too late — convert before adding. Go vs Rust Rust panics on overflow in debug builds and wraps (with wrapping_add / checked_add / overflowing_add options) in release. Go always wraps, in every build mode. Idiomatic Go returns (value, ok) or (value, overflow bool); idiomatic Rust returns Option via checked_add.
Trivia The most famous overflow bug is Ariane 5 flight 501 (1996): a 64-bit float converted to a 16-bit int overflowed and crashed the guidance computer. Smaller scale, same lesson — never trust a narrowing conversion.
Tip: when you see uint8, uint16, or byte arithmetic, ask “can this wrap?” If yes, use sum < a, math/bits, or a wider type before shipping.

Div Mod Go functions can return multiple values, so quotient and remainder come back together: func DivMod(a, b int) (int, int). Integer / truncates toward zero and % gives the remainder with the sign of the dividend.

title: Floats
content:
Floats float64 holds fractional numbers. Converting after integer division keeps the truncation: float64(5/2) is 2.0, while float64(5)/2 is 2.5. The math package (math.Pi, math.Sqrt) covers the rest.

title: Runes
content:
Runes A Go string is bytes; a rune is one character. "é" is 2 bytes (len reports 2) but a single rune. Indexing a string yields bytes — ranging over it yields runes.
Task Fix CountRunes in calc.go so multibyte characters count once.

title: Strings
content:
Strings Strings support == and +, but you cannot assign to an index: s[0] = 'H' does not compile. Build a new string with slicing and concatenation instead. The strings package has the rest.

title: Bitwise operators
content:
Bitwise operators << shifts bits, &/|/^ combine them. With iota, each constant in a block gets a successive value, so 1 << iota builds power-of-two flags that combine with | and test with &.
